For fifty years the cricket pavilion at Askerby sat at the bottom of the village field, a few yards from the river Lume: a plain timber building of 1911, with a veranda, two changing rooms and a tea room. In March 1962 a gale tore away half its roof. The committee met in April, and the secretary, Moira Callan, wrote down nearly every word.

The first thing discussed was the river. In 1947 the Lume had lain a foot deep in the changing rooms for three days, and when it drained away the pavilion was still square on its footings, hardly a board sprung. The building, members told one another, had survived worse. Money was a separate worry. The club had been in debt since 1958, when a new scoreboard cost twice what Harlan Dace, the builder, had quoted, and rot was already in its posts.

Dace came with an offer. He worked mostly in brick, he said, but the timber was worth forty pounds to him if the club would sell. Tobias Fenn, the groundsman, remarked that forty pounds would pay for moving the scoreboard to higher ground. Then the captain, Neil Pryor, took a stand. He had climbed into the roof with a lamp that morning: the rafters were sound, the gale had taken only the sheeting, and the members could repair it themselves for the price of a summer's teas.

The vote was eleven to two for Pryor's plan. Through May the members worked on Saturdays, and Agnes Rowe, the headmistress, let them use the village school hall on weekday evenings to cut and paint the new boards. By June the roof was whole again, on the same building and the same footings, a few yards from the same river.

The roof those members nailed down is still on the pavilion, sixty years and many gales later. Anyone who sits on its veranda on a match day is sitting under the work of a village that looked hard at its own building, trusted what it found, and was proved right.

passage:
Last October the Brannock Reservoir dropped two meters in four days, so that Hester Vane, the engineer in charge of the dam, could repair its gates on the schedule she had set. The drop would leave Hollin Cove, a shallow arm with a worn gravel bar across its mouth, nearly dry; only the old river channel would stay deep. On the cove's floor lived some four thousand mussels, counted that summer by the biologist Ilse Marrow and her student Teo Arlan. A mussel can follow a falling waterline on its single foot, but slowly, about a meter a day.

The reservoir had been lowered once before, twenty years earlier, and Bram Kettle, a fisherman from Wendle, recorded it in the logbook he has kept for thirty years. The water fell just as fast that time. Within a week, his log says, nearly every mussel stranded in the cove had died, and he counted eleven still alive among the gulls.

It was Kettle who proposed the plan the team followed. He raised nine hundred dollars in Wendle for buckets and waders, and on the first morning forty volunteers waded in behind him to carry mussels from the shrinking shallows to the channel. Teo had sketched a wall of sandbags across the cove's mouth, but there was money for one plan, and Kettle's was already moving. Odile Prask, who runs the breeding hatchery at Sallow Ford, took two hundred mussels into her tanks as a reserve.

By the fourth evening the volunteers had moved more than three thousand. Marrow left a few hundred alone in a corner too soft to wade and counted them ten days later; fewer than twenty had lived. In the channel, nine in ten of her tagged mussels came through the winter.

What stands out in Marrow's notes is the arithmetic of the rescue: forty people, four days, three thousand mussels, each one lifted by hand. Her report lists every volunteer by name, which seems the least such an effort has earned.
